credits.readme:
No libraries. Background plate generated with Midjourney for Taste and
retouched; the salema is Diego Delso's photograph (Catania, 2025, CC BY-SA 4.0,
Wikimedia Commons), cut out (see `assets/credits.json`). Sounds synthesised in Python for this
component. Physics after Luhar and Nepf (2011, Limnol. Oceanogr. 56; 2016, J.
Fluids Struct. 61), Ghisalberti and Nepf (2002, J. Geophys. Res. 107), Stuart
(1967, J. Fluid Mech. 29); caustics after Evan Wallace's WebGL Water (2011).

files.text:
Five metres down, in the Posidonia

seagrass meadow
The swell

Each passing wave moves the water near the bed back and forth, so the leaves sway with it every six seconds or so, and lie over further when a set comes through.

Monami

A slow current shears over the top of the canopy and rolls up into vortices. As each one passes, a wave of bending runs across the meadow.

The salema

Almost nothing eats the living leaf. The salema does: a school drifts in over the meadow, a fish drops to a leaf tip for two or three twisting bites, and swims back up into its place.

seagrass-meadow

# seagrass-meadow A hero band five metres down in a Mediterranean Posidonia meadow on a sunny day. You lie on the pale sand and look along it: ribbons of leaf a centimetre wide rise around you, lean and sway back with every swell, and every so often a wave of bending rolls across the meadow as a vortex passes over the canopy. A net of sunlight crawls over the sand and up the leaves, shafts hang in the water, specks of marine snow drift back and forth with the surge, and the far meadow fades into blue. Move your hand through it and the leaves part around it and trail after it in the wake. ```html ``` ```js import { seagrassMeadow } from './seagrass-meadow.js'; const destroy = seagrassMeadow(figure, { surge: 0.09, current: 0.12, species: 'zostera' }); destroy.pause(); // stop (the visitor's pause button does the same) destroy.play(); await destroy.sweep(); // a hand swept through the meadow, left to right destroy.advance(3); // run the simulation 3 s ahead at once (tests, stills) destroy.state; // 'live' | 'paused' | 'idle' (offscreen, hidden tab) | 'still' (reduced motion) destroy.renderer; // 'webgl' or 'canvas' destroy(); // remove everything, leave the plain figure ``` Without JS it is the ``: the open-water plate, sunlit from above. ## How it works ### The leaves Each leaf near the camera (about 1000 on a desktop, 520 on a phone) is a chain of eight segments rooted in the sand, simulated in SI units at 90 Hz with the forces used for flexible seagrass by Luhar and Nepf (2011, 2016): - **Buoyancy.** Posidonia leaves are full of air channels (aerenchyma), so the leaf is lighter than water and stands up in still water. Net lift per unit length is Δρ g b t, with Δρ = 300 kg/m³, width b of 8 to 10.5 mm and thickness t = 0.4 mm. - **Bending stiffness.** EI = E b t³/12 with E = 0.45 GPa, about 2.3 × 10⁻⁵ N m². Each joint is a couple: it swings the nodes either side of it back toward a straight line and the joint takes the reaction. - **Drag** on the component of the relative flow *normal* to the leaf, ½ ρ C_D b |u_n| u_n with C_D = 1.95 (a flat plate), plus skin friction along it. Because only the normal flow pushes, a leaf that bends over sheds load: that is reconfiguration, and it is why the meadow leans into a current instead of snapping. The drag is integrated exactly (exponential relaxation toward the water's velocity), so a fast hand cannot make it unstable. - **Added mass and inertia.** A leaf drags a cylinder of water with it (C_A ρ π b²/4 per metre), which dominates its mass, and the accelerating water of the swell pushes on it (the Morison inertia force). - Segment lengths are held by a follow-the-leader projection from the root, and leaves cannot go through the sand, and are eased out of the hand. A little internal (tissue) damping between neighbouring nodes keeps the chain from zig-zagging when the hand drags it. At the defaults a 0.6 m leaf has a buoyancy number B = Δρ g b t L³/EI ≈ 100 and a Cauchy number Ca = ½ ρ C_D b U² L³/EI ≈ 650 in the swell, so drag wins and the leaves lean well over at each peak. But the water's excursion each half wave, A = U T / 2π ≈ 8 cm, is far shorter than the leaf, so the upper leaf mostly rides back and forth with the water and the lower leaf stays put: the motion is the characteristic swaying of a meadow in waves, not a flag in a wind. Leaves grow in shoots of four to seven, fanned in one plane (distichous), the outer ones oldest and longest. Each leaf turns its flat face to the flow and bends about its weak axis, and twists a little along its length. Beyond about 3 m, 6000 more leaves (3000 on a phone) are drawn by the GPU from the steady answer of the same balance: the tip rides the orbital excursion of the swell, and leans by drag against buoyancy in the local current. ### The water The velocity at any point is the sum of three things. 1. **Swell.** Three linear waves with periods near 6.2 s and slightly different headings. Each one's wavenumber comes from the dispersion relation ω² = g k tanh(k h) at h = 5 m (wavelength about 40 m), and its near-bed orbital velocity U is set by `surge`. Their beating gives sets: every minute or so a few bigger waves come through. The phase k·x travels across the meadow at about 6 m/s, so each surge sweeps across rather than arriving everywhere at once. Inside the canopy it is damped by about a fifth. 2. **Current and monami.** A weak current flows above the canopy and much less within it (here 25 %), so there is a shear layer at the canopy top. Such a layer is unstable and rolls up into a row of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortices that travel at the mean of the two speeds (Ghisalberti and Nepf 2002). It is modelled with Stuart's (1967) exact solution for a periodic row of vortices in a mixing layer: concentration ρ = 0 gives the plain tanh profile, and as ρ rises toward 1 the vorticity gathers into cores. Each vortex sweeps fast water down into the canopy on its leading side and lifts it on its trailing side, so the leaves under it bow and recover in turn: a wave of bending that travels with the vortices, which is what monami is. Wavelength 0.95 m. The vortices come in trains of three or four, their crests wobble across the meadow, and trains grow and fade. 3. **Your hand.** A sphere 10 cm across, its speed capped at a swimmer's 1 m/s. Around it, the potential-flow dipole of a moving sphere pushes water (and leaves) aside ahead and draws it in behind; leaves touching it are pushed out. Every 3 cm of travel it leaves a puff of momentum (0.4 of the hand's velocity) that spreads as it ages, decays in under a second and drifts with the swell, so leaves keep moving after the hand has gone. Marine snow (a few hundred particles, 0.6 to 3 mm, sinking 1.2 mm/s) is moved by the same water, which is the best way to see the swell is back and forth. ### The light - **Caustics.** A periodic heightfield of ten gravity-capillary ripples (wavelengths 18 to 47 cm, slopes about 0.01 each, ω² = g k + (σ/ρ) k³), plus the slope of the long swell, which sways the whole net back and forth in time with the surge. A 88² grid of the surface refracts the sun (Snell, n = 1.333) down 5 m to the floor; each triangle's brightness is the ratio of its area before and after (after Evan Wallace's WebGL Water). The sun's disc, half a degree, blurs the net by about 4 cm at this depth, so it is never sampled finer than that. - **Shafts.** The view ray is marched through the water and, at each step, the caustic net is looked up along the sun's direction: the shafts are the caustic beams themselves, so they flicker with the net and converge toward the sun. Henyey-Greenstein forward scattering (g = 0.72) makes them strongest looking toward the sun. - **Sun.** 62° above the horizon in air; refracted, 69° under water, inside Snell's window, ahead and to the left like the plate's own rays. Its colour at 5 m loses red fastest (diffuse attenuation 0.15, 0.05, 0.04 per metre), then is white-balanced the way the plate (and any diver's camera) is, so the leaves and sand sit in the photograph's colour rather than the eye's. - **Distance.** Every surface is attenuated by Beer-Lambert per channel (0.42, 0.15, 0.13 per metre) and filled in by the water's colour, read from the plate at the horizon straight behind it, so the far meadow fades into the blue of the photograph rather than into a guessed colour. - **Leaves.** Lit by the caustic sun (less of it deeper in the canopy), a sky and sand ambient, and light passing *through* the leaf, which comes out greener-yellow and is strongest looking toward the sun. Close up they show their parallel veins. They age from the tip: older (outer) leaves brown at the tip with a ragged boundary, carry a film of epiphytes toward the tip and small pink-white crusts of coralline algae. The base is the brown sheath. - **Sand.** Pale carbonate sand with grain and mottling, darker with litter under the meadow, symmetric wave ripples in the open sand (crests across the surge, wavelength about 0.65 of the orbital diameter), the caustic net, and the leaves' own shadows projected along the sun and fading with height. ### The salema The one Mediterranean fish that grazes Posidonia itself, *Sarpa salpa*, now visits. A school of 34 (22 on a phone) comes in from one side about four seconds after the meadow starts, cruises over the canopy, grazes for about half a minute and leaves by the other side; the next visit comes 30 to 55 s later. Each fish follows the three zones of Couzin et al. (2002): repulsion under 15 cm, alignment to 60 cm, attraction to 1.5 m, plus the school's heading; turning is rate-limited, speed eases, and the tail beats at f ≈ U / 0.6 L (Bainbridge), faster and wider when bolting. While the school grazes, a fish now and then drops to the nearest simulated leaf tip, pitches head-down, takes three twisting bites (each bite tugs that leaf in the simulation, so you see it pulled) and rises back. A hand moving faster than 0.25 m/s within 55 cm makes a fish bolt away from it, and the fright passes to its neighbours a beat later. Nothing steers them toward the pointer. Each fish is one real photographed salema (`assets/salema.webp`, cut out of Diego Delso's photograph), drawn in the 3D scene as a vertical card along its heading, so it foreshortens to a sliver as it turns toward you; the rear body sweeps across the card's plane with each beat. It is lit like the leaves (the caustic net crawls over its back), sunk into the water by the same Beer-Lambert fog, and depth-tested against the leaves, so a grazing fish disappears among them. ### The plate The Midjourney image supplies the water column and the surface: the window of sky, the bright surface, its rays and the blue distance. Its grass was masked and inpainted out (only the water above the horizon is used) and the sand is drawn in 3D, so that the caustics, shadows and leaves share one perspective. The camera is matched to it: 52° vertical field, eye 30 cm above the sand, pitched up so the floor's horizon falls on the plate's horizon. The surface in the plate wobbles a little with the same ripples that make the caustics. ## In the page The water is a crisp band, but the canvas rises above it by `--sm-rise` (30 % of the band's height; 20 % on phones), so the leaves nearest you grow up past the band's top edge onto the paper and sway there, behind the page's own text (the canvas takes no pointer events; give the heading above `position: relative; z-index: 1` and leave some space above the band). Only the leaves leave the water: the plate, the fish and the marine snow stop at its edge, and the risen leaves thin out at the canvas's sides and top instead of ending on a cut line. - **Your hand.** A mouse anywhere over the band or the risen leaves, or a finger dragged sideways on the band, is a hand in the water: the leaves part around it, trail after it and spring back with their own damping. A vertical swipe still scrolls. - **Scroll is current.** The page's scroll speed stirs a current along the band (up to 0.16 m/s) that the near leaves and the far meadow lean into, and it slackens within a second of the page stopping. - **The fish.** A pointer sweeping past a salema on screen (faster than about 140 px/s, within a tenth of the band's width) sends it off into the blue; the fright spreads and the school closes up again. They never follow it. - **Rest.** The sea is up while someone is here: when the band scrolls into view, while the page is scrolled, while a hand is in the water. After `idle` seconds (24) of none of that the swell dies away, the vortices stop rolling, the caustics and the specks of snow come to a stop, the school moves on, and once no leaf is moving the loop stops (`state` becomes `'resting'`). Any scroll or touch brings it back. ## Options Data attributes, or the options object (which wins). | Option | Attribute | Default | | |---|---|---|---| | `plate` | `data-plate` | the ``'s src, else `assets/meadow-plate.webp` | Background plate (water and surface; horizon at 55.4 % down, 16:9). | | `species` | `data-species` | `posidonia` | `zostera`: narrower (3 to 5.5 mm), thinner, shorter leaves in shoots of three to five. | | `blades` | `data-blades` | `0` (auto: 1000, phone 520, canvas 240) | Simulated leaves. | | `far` | `data-far` | `0` (auto: 6000, phone 3000) | Quasi-static far leaves (WebGL only). | | `snow` | `data-snow` | `0` (auto: 280, phone 160) | Marine snow particles. | | `surge` | `data-surge` | `0.085` | Near-bed orbital velocity of the swell, m/s. 0 for a still day (monami only). | | `period` | `data-period` | `6.2` | Dominant swell period, s. | | `current` | `data-current` | `0.065` | Current above the canopy, m/s. Drives the lean and the monami. | | `depth` | `data-depth` | `5` | Water depth, m (wave dispersion, caustic focus, light colour). | | `heading` | `data-heading` | `18` | Swell direction, degrees from screen right toward the distance. Tilt turns it. | | `paused` | `data-paused` | off | Start paused. | | `label` | `data-label` | a description | Accessible name of the canvas. | | `fish` | `data-fish` | auto: 34, phone 22 | Salema in the school; 0 for none. | | `fishImg` | | `assets/salema.webp` | The fish cut-out. | | `idle` | `data-idle` | `24` | Seconds without scroll or touch before the sea goes slack and the loop stops. | Events (bubbling): `seagrass-meadow:surge` once per wave as the flow turns shoreward, `detail.size` is `'big'` or `'small'`; `seagrass-meadow:swish` when the hand moves fast. `sounds.json` plays a synthesised underwater surge on the first and a soft swish on the second (off until the visitor turns sound on). ## Theming | Variable | Default | | |---|---|---| | `--sm-aspect` | `21 / 9` | Band shape (the camera crops the plate to it). | | `--sm-aspect-narrow` | `4 / 5` | Band shape at 640px and below. | | `--sm-rise` / `--sm-rise-narrow` | `30%` / `20%` | How far above the band the leaves may grow (of the band's height). | | `--sm-radius` | `0` | Corner radius. | | `--sm-water` | `#1b6e78` | Colour behind everything before the plate loads. | | `--sm-control` | pale aqua | The pause button's ink. | ## Accessibility The canvas is `role="img"` with a description of the scene (`label`).
